2.text: Ceremonial of Heads. — Early in summer, as soon as the catch of the

3.text: seals on the drifting ice is finished, the ceremonial of heads takes place.

4.text: This, likewise, is performed by the boat-owners with the participation of the

5.text: crew, and the details have many points of resemblance to the ceremonial of

6.text: wild reindeer-heads among the Reindeer Chukchee.¹ It is even called by the

8.text: The heads of the walrus and of the thong-seal are the only ones stored

9.text: for this ceremonial, while of the smaller seals only a couple or so are taken

10.text: for the exhibition. When walrus-heads are scarce, the ceremonial is con-

11.text: sidered very poor, and even of no importance. In the morning of the day,

12.text: all the heads are brought from the blubber-hole, and exposed on the skins

13.text: in the middle of the house. A large lamp, placed on a flat stone, stands

14.text: with them; and a little at one side a small piˊntᴇ fire² is arranged, which is

15.text: wanting in the ceremonial of the Asiatic Eskimo. All kinds of “alien”

16.text: food — sausage, reindeer-tallow, tobacco, flour — are produced for the sac-

17.text: rifice and put near the heads. Then the old woman presiding over the

18.text: ceremonial sits down before the heads and begins to sing, one by one, the tunes

19.text: of the family; while the male members of the family go around the heads,

20.text: exclaiming, “Yoho, yoho!” in the usual manner. The old woman feeds the

21.text: lamp, and keeps up the fire; while the men, with plates filled with provisions,

22.text: go out to offer sacrifice to all the directions, beginning, as usual, with the

23.text: morning dawn, then passing to the zenith, to the nadir, and after that to

25.text: The other members of the crew stay in the house and are the onlookers.

26.text: When those who performed the sacrifice are returning, the largest walrus-

27.text: head is tied up with a long rope, which all the men grasp, pretending to

28.text: haul in the captured walrus. This symbolizes a successful catch for the future.

29.text: The old woman gives of the provisions which served for the sacrifice to the

30.text: women present, who, as said before, are the oldest representatives of the

32.text: The ceremonial dance is performed in the usual way. A man with the

33.text: drum stands on the outer side of the group of heads, having his back turned

34.text: to the entrance; while the women dancers stand opposite to him, on the inner

35.text: side of the heads. The movements of the dancers are of the usual character;

36.text: that is, they make a short courtesy, then stand erect and turn their bodies to

37.text: the right and to the left, all the while never stepping aside from their place.

38.text: Among the Asiatic Eskimo, however, this dance alternates from time to time

39.text: with a more active form, in which the dancer performs a series of jumps,

40.text: swinging violently both his arms over his head. This latter variety of dance

41.text: is, however, considered an imitation of the dance of the natives of St. Law-
